issue.issue_text: When penal action can be taken under both the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which statute would prevail.

facts: The alleged offense of misbranding a food product occurred on November 29, 2010.
On this date, provisions of both the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA) and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA) were in force.
The PFA was not fully repealed until August 5, 2011.
However, Section 89 of the FSSA, which gives the Act an overriding effect, was brought into force on July 29, 2010, prior to the offense.
There was a conflict in the punishment for misbranding: the PFA prescribed imprisonment and a fine, while the FSSA prescribed only a monetary penalty.
law: Section 16 of the PFA made misbranding a criminal offense punishable with imprisonment.
Section 52 of the FSSA provides for a monetary penalty for misbranded food, but no imprisonment.

Section 89 of the FSSA contains a non-obstante clause stating that its provisions shall have effect "notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force."
application: The Court identified a clear inconsistency between the two statutes regarding the punishment for misbranding. The PFA treated it as a criminal offense requiring imprisonment, while the FSSA treated it as a violation subject only to a monetary penalty.
The Court focused on the effect of Section 89 of the FSSA, which was already in force at the time of the alleged offense.

It reasoned that this 'overriding effect' clause was specifically designed to resolve such conflicts. Because the penalty under the PFA was inconsistent with the penalty under the FSSA, the FSSA's provision must prevail.
Therefore, even though the PFA had not yet been formally repealed, its penal provision for misbranding was rendered ineffective by the overriding power of Section 89 of the FSSA.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that where there is an inconsistency between the two statutes, the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA) would prevail. This is due to the overriding effect of Section 89 of the FSSA, which was in force at the time of the offense. Consequently, the prosecution of the appellant under the PFA was invalid and was quashed.

arguments.issue_text: When penal action can be taken under both the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, which statute would prevail.
appellant_arguments: In view of Section 89 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA), which gives the Act an overriding effect, Rule 32 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules will have no application, even if it was in force on the date of the alleged violation.
The respondent could not proceed under the provisions of the PFA merely because the rules corresponding to Rule 32 of the PFA Rules had not yet been notified under the FSSA regime.
This is especially true given that Section 97 of the FSSA, which repeals the PFA, was brought into force with effect from 29th July 2010.
respondent_arguments: The acts or omissions constituting the alleged offence took place when the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA) was not repealed, even though the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA) was in force.
Rule 32 of the PFA Rules, the violation of which is alleged, was also in force on the date of the offence.
Sub-section (4) of Section 97 of the FSSA permits cognizance of an offence under the PFA for up to three years from the date of the commencement of the FSSA.
Considering the principles in Section 97(4) of the FSSA, the prosecution for violating the provisions of the PFA and its Rules is maintainable.
After the FSSA came into force, all provisions of the PFA and the PFA Rules continued to apply.
Even the Rules under the FSSA, as per Section 52, were not brought into force at the relevant time, which supports the continued application of the PFA Rules.

statutes.section: Unnamed Section (4) in the text, likely Section 97(4)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: By virtue of Section 89 of the Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA), its provisions have an overriding effect over anything inconsistent contained in any other food-related law in force, including the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) and its rules. Consequently, a rule under the PFA will have no application if it is inconsistent with the FSSA.
obiter: There are other arguments made by the learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant. But we need not deal with the same as the appellant must succeed on the abovementioned grounds.
